body: I guess there's another related subtlety, which is, can the parser create custom elements when there is a parser blocking script? Probably not. Twiddling the stack of open formatting elements comes to mind, but I guess that cannot happen when processing a close script tag because script tags are processed in text mode?

Here's an example of a subtle interaction with the parser pause flag:

If, in a script, you document.write a custom element then I believe its constructor will set the parser pause flag and on exit, not un-set it (because the script nesting level has been incremented for the first script, hence is non-zero.) Then subsequent calls to document.write will halt and unwind at the tokenization stage, because the parser pause flag is set. (I wonder if custom element running should save and restore the state of the parser pause flag?)

So this was lifted from https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#parsing-main-inforeign:parser-pause-flag, which basically is trying to disallow `document.write` in SVG script elements. It says

> Process the SVG script element according to the SVG rules, if the user agent supports SVG. [SVG]
> 
> Even if this causes new characters to be inserted into the tokenizer, the parser will not be executed reentrantly, since the parser pause flag is true.

That is where I got this from. But maybe the ignore-destructive-writes-counter would be more straightforward.

---

> Maybe the note could be more specific about the relationship between the parser blocking script, tokenization and the parser pause flag. That is, a parser blocking script is only set when processing an end script tag token; if the tokenizer is blocked, then the parser blocking script cannot be set. (I hope that is right?)

I think I see what you're saying. To me the biggest thing to be clarified is how the parser pause flag impacts document.write. It's clear that pending parser-blocking scripts will stop it in its tracks, but the fact that setting the parser pause flag will also do so (by making the nested tokenization invocation immediately abort) is not written down in this note. So I'm thinking to change the note to

> If the document.write() method was called from script executing inline (i.e. executing because the parser parsed a set of script tags), then this is a reentrant invocation of the parser. If the parser pause flag is set, the tokenizer will abort immediately and no HTML will be parsed, per the definition of the parser pause flag.

---

> I guess there's another related subtlety, which is, can the parser create custom elements when there is a parser blocking script? Probably not.

Yeah, I agree this cannot happen.

> If, in a script, you document.write a custom element then I believe its constructor will set the parser pause flag and on exit, not un-set it (because the script nesting level has been incremented for the first script, hence is non-zero.) Then subsequent calls to document.write will halt and unwind at the tokenization stage, because the parser pause flag is set. (I wonder if custom element running should save and restore the state of the parser pause flag?)

This seems kind of bad. I think we could fix this by using the "ignore-destructive-writes counter" instead of the parser pause flag.

Alternately, we could go more drastic and say that document.write() must always do upgrades, similar to the fragment parsing algorithm. (That is, reentrant invocations of the parser set "will execute script" to false.) What do you think of that?

My gut tells me that document.write should not '"must" do upgrades.' document.write may cause very little to happen (no-op, raise exception) or a lot to happen (feed tokenizer, cause parsing, etc.) and layering a requirement that happens deep in that pipeline seems wrong. It would be easier to be consistent if document.write fed the tokenizer and let custom elements unfold as a natural extension of that.

I think we should turn the question back around and concentrate more on what document.write does when it is used in a parser-created custom element constructor/callback. Script tags interact with document.write; arguably so should custom elements. If you squint they are another script-running mechanism.
@dominiccooney you might want to restate that in #1630 or https://github.com/w3c/webcomponents/issues/537 if you haven't already as this issue was only used to clarify the note.
